checks.claim: Dial painters in New Jersey (USRC, Orange, 1917-1926) and Illinois (Radium Dial, Ottawa, from 1922); 'from about 1917'
checks.note: Grokipedia: Orange plant operated 1917 to 1926 (Grace Fryer began 10 April 1917); Ottawa plant from September 1922. 'From about 1917' is true of the trade as a whole; the Illinois plant began in 1922, so 'from about 1917' read as applying to both states is loose but not false. Optional tightening: 'from 1917 in New Jersey and 1922 in Illinois'.

checks.claim: Taught to point brushes with their lips; told the paint was harmless
checks.note: Wikipedia: instructed to 'point' brushes on their lips; 'The workers had been told the paint was harmless.' Grokipedia: repeatedly licked brushes; company gave 'expert assurances of its harmlessness'.

checks.claim: Key: the body builds radium into bone as it does calcium
checks.note: Grokipedia, Radium: skeletal uptake by 'its chemical analogy to calcium', substituting for calcium in hydroxyapatite. AHF: 'The human body mistakes radium for calcium, so it filled their bones'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: red blood cells (iron), thyroid (iodine), body fat (fat-soluble vitamins) are each wrong for radium
checks.note: Radium is a bone seeker; it is not concentrated in red cells, thyroid or fat. Each analogy is true of its own element (iron in haemoglobin, iodine in thyroid, A/D/E/K in fat and liver).

checks.claim: Context: radium is in the same periodic-table column as calcium (group 2, alkaline earths)
checks.note: Grokipedia: radium belongs to the alkaline earth metals, group 2 (calcium's group).

checks.claim: Context: radium-226 half-life about 1,600 years; alpha emitter irradiating nearby cells
checks.note: Grokipedia: half-life approximately 1,600 years; decays primarily by alpha emission to radon-222.

checks.claim: Arthur Roeder, USRC president, contacted Cecil Drinker of the Harvard School of Public Health
checks.note: Harvard Chan School: 'Company President Arthur Roeder contacted industrial hygiene expert Cecil Drinker to investigate'.

checks.claim: Plant saturated with radium dust; Drinker judged radium was making the women ill
checks.note: 'saturated with radium-contaminated dust'; Drinker concluded continuous radium exposure caused the women's health problems.

checks.claim: Roeder blamed an infection caught outside the factory
checks.note: Roeder 'insisted that a contagious infection contracted outside the factory must be to blame'.

checks.claim: Key: USRC sent the NJ Department of Labor Drinker's report altered to say all were well
checks.note: Harvard: USRC submitted Drinker's report to the NJ Department of Labor 'with the findings altered'; Hamilton's letter: the department's copy 'shows that every girl is in perfect condition'. Wikipedia, Radium Girls: 'the results altered to show the company in a better light'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: unaltered report; altered to blame infection; nothing sent
checks.note: All contradicted: the report was sent, and altered to show health, not to blame an infection (no source says the altered copy named an infection).

checks.claim: Context: Alice Hamilton, Harvard expert on industrial poisons; 1925 letter to Katherine Drinker with the quoted words 'every girl is in perfect condition' and 'a forged report in your name'
checks.note: Harvard quotes the letter: 'it shows that every girl is in perfect condition. Do you suppose Roeder could do such a thing as to issue a forged report in your name?' Hamilton was Drinker's HSPH colleague and author of Industrial Poisons in the United States (1925; NLM https://www.nlm.nih.gov/exhibition/thisleadiskillingus/collection-transcript5.html).

checks.claim: Context: Roeder threatened to sue and never showed the internal report; the Drinkers published
checks.note: Roeder cited an internal report refuting Drinker but refused to show it; 'Roeder threatened to sue'; the Drinkers 'ignored the continued threat of a lawsuit and published the report'.

checks.claim: Grace Fryer and four others settled with USRC in 1928
checks.note: Coursey (J. Res. NIST 2021) and Grokipedia: settled 4 June 1928 (Wikipedia says autumn 1928); '1928' is safe either way. Plaintiffs Fryer, Hussman, Schaub, McDonald, Larice.

checks.claim: Catherine Donohue won her case against Radium Dial in Illinois in 1938
checks.note: Arbitrator ruled for her on 5 April 1938; Illinois Industrial Commission upheld it 6 July 1938.

checks.claim: Robley Evans, MIT physicist, studied former dial painters in the 1930s
checks.note: DOE: 'In the early 30s at MIT, Evans investigated the bioeffects of radium on dial painters'; first exhaled-radon measurement 1933 (Wikipedia, Radium Girls).

checks.claim: 'A committee he chaired set the first tolerance level for radium workers in 1941'
checks.note: The 1941 level was published in NBS Handbook 27 (May 1941); Coursey (J. Res. NIST 2021): 'Curtiss chaired the advisory committee that prepared this handbook', with Evans a member; the H27 front matter lists L. F. Curtiss as chairman (https://nvlpubs.nist.gov/nistpubs/Legacy/hb/nbshandbook27.pdf). Evans proposed the 0.1 figure and polled the other members (Wikipedia, Robley D. Evans (physicist)). Only the DOE ACHRE report (chap5_1) calls Evans 'the committee chairman'. Fix: 'A National Bureau of Standards committee he sat on adopted his proposal for the first tolerance level, in 1941' (or 'Evans proposed the first tolerance level, adopted in 1941').

checks.claim: Key: it capped the radium held in a worker's body (body burden); wrong choices (handled per day, per paint pot, per dial) are wrong
checks.note: ACHRE: '0.1 microgram fixed in the body should be the tolerance level for radium'; Coursey: 'the limit of 0.1 ug for the body burden of radium'.

checks.claim: Context: 0.1 microgram
checks.note: H27/Coursey and DOE give 0.1 microgram; Wikipedia gives 0.1 microcurie. For radium-226 one gram is about one curie, so the two are the same amount; 'microgram' is the handbook's own unit.

checks.claim: Context: Evans judged no bone cancers below 0.1 microgram
checks.note: 'Evans judged that there would be no bone cancers below 0.1 microgram 226Ra in the skeleton.'

checks.claim: Context: a breath test for radon (radium's decay gas) could check a living worker
checks.note: Exhaled-air samples counted for radon-222 measured body radium (DOE fn. 93; Evans 1933; Hughes's breath tests of 1927-28 in Coursey).

checks.claim: Context: Manhattan Project's first plutonium body limit came by comparison with radium; safety rules patterned on a radium dial plant
checks.note: ACHRE: the tentative plutonium level 'was derived by direct comparison of the relative energies of plutonium and radium'. AHF (https://ahf.nuclearmuseum.org/ahf/history/radium-girls/): Hempelmann recalled visiting a Boston radium dial plant; procedures 'patterned after that'.

checks.claim: Chemie Grunenthal began selling thalidomide (Contergan) as a sleeping pill in West Germany in 1957, at first over the counter
checks.note: Wikipedia: launched 1 October 1957 as Contergan; 'available as an over-the-counter drug' in West Germany until neuritis reports from late 1959. Grokipedia: a sedative for insomnia.

checks.claim: Its advertising called it non-toxic
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'claiming it was non-toxic even at high doses'. A 1957 Grunenthal circular stressed 'completely non-poisonous' and 'atoxicity proved in animal experiments' (Sydney Morning Herald via https://www.newspapers.com/newspage/120693749/; Open Book Publishers ch. 18).

checks.claim: Key: rats and mice survived huge doses
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'no lethal effects even at doses exceeding 10 grams per kilogram in rodents'. Open Book Publishers ch. 18: oral doses above 5,000 mg/kg failed to kill mice (https://books.openbookpublishers.com/10.11647/obp.0055/Ch-18.xhtml).

checks.claim: Wrong choices: monkeys for months; pregnant animals with healthy young; many pregnant women safely
checks.note: 'Reproductive toxicity testing in pregnant animals was not conducted'; never tested on pregnant women (Wikipedia, Thalidomide scandal); no primate study behind the claim.

checks.claim: Context: rodent-only tests were usual at the time; never tried in pregnant women though given for morning sickness
checks.note: 'They were tested for toxicity on rodents only, as was usual at the time'; Thalidomide scandal: introduced for morning sickness 'without having been tested on pregnant women'. (Grokipedia lists other species in Grunenthal's early tests; the rodent claim is the one the advertising rested on.)

checks.claim: Context: rats and mice far less sensitive than rabbits and some monkeys to harm to the unborn
checks.note: Rodents 'proved insensitive to the drug's impact on limb development at typical doses'; phocomelia in 'New Zealand white rabbits and certain primates'.

checks.claim: Context: late 1961 Lenz and McBride linked it to shortened or missing limbs; Grunenthal withdrew it
checks.note: Lenz alerted Grunenthal 15 November 1961; withdrawn from the German market 26 November 1961; McBride's Lancet letter 16 December 1961 (his suspicion was raised earlier in 1961).

checks.claim: Kelsey joined the FDA in August 1960; Richardson-Merrell's thalidomide (Kevadon) application among her first
checks.note: Joined 1 August 1960; application submitted 8 September 1960 (Grokipedia); 'one of the first' (FDA exhibit).

checks.claim: First sent back in November 1960
checks.note: Her 10 November 1960 letter deemed the application incomplete, resetting the 60-day clock (Scientific American 2024; Grokipedia).

checks.claim: Key: it had not been shown to be safe
checks.note: FDA: refused 'because of its inadequate evidence'; UChicago Medicine 2020: 'insisted on hard evidence to back Merrell's claims for the drug's safety'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: already harmed babies in Europe; killed patients by overdose; failed to help sleep
checks.note: The birth-defect link came about a year later (late 1961); no lethal dose was known; efficacy was not a requirement of the 1938 law and not her ground.

checks.claim: Context: file leaned on doctors' praise over clinical data; shaky absorption figures; unfinished animal studies
checks.note: Grokipedia: 'testimonials rather than controlled studies', 'inconsistent pharmacokinetic data on absorption', 'incomplete animal experiments'; UChicago: 'anecdotal testimony in place of clinical data'.

checks.claim: Context: 'Under the law of the day she could turn a drug down only by proving it unsafe'
checks.note: Weinberger v. Hynson (US Supreme Court, 1973) on the 1938 Act: the FDA could refuse an application on 'finding that it could not determine from existing evidence or had not been shown that it was safe'; the catch was that an application 'automatically became effective if it was not disapproved' within the deadline. UChicago Medicine 2020: she rejected it four times 'on the grounds of insufficient data'; her own 5 May 1961 letter (quoted in 00cf2f4370's card) put 'the burden of proof that the drug is safe' on the applicant, so this line also contradicts the next card. Only Scientific American 2024 says she had to prove it unsafe. Fix: 'Under the law of the day the application would take effect by itself after 60 days unless the FDA acted, so she declared it incomplete again and again and asked for more.'

checks.claim: A. Leslie Florence's letter in the British Medical Journal (31 December 1960, 'Is thalidomide to blame?')
checks.note: Scientific American: Scottish doctor Leslie Florence, 'Is Thalidomide to Blame?', BMJ, December 1960 (BMJ 1960;2(5217):1953-4, dated 31 December 1960); Kelsey read it in late January or early February 1961, while still holding the application.

checks.claim: Four patients taking it nightly for over a year; numbness and tingling in hands and feet (nerve damage)
checks.note: 'Each of the four patients had been taking a nightly dose of thalidomide for more than a year'; paresthesia beginning in the feet, then the hands; peripheral neuritis.

checks.claim: Key: the letter led her to ask for proof it was safe for unborn babies
checks.note: UChicago: the letter 'prompted Kelsey to request, with grim prescience, proof the drug was not harmful to the fetus'; Wikipedia: she 'also requested animal studies to demonstrate that the drug would not be harmful to the fetus'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: better than older pills; not habit-forming; no harm to the liver
checks.note: None is named in any account as the request the letter prompted; comparative efficacy was not a legal requirement.

checks.claim: Context: nerve damage not what she expected of a simple sleeping pill
checks.note: WETA (from her memoir): it 'did not seem the [sort] of side effect that should come from a simple sleeping pill'. Paraphrased in the card, correctly not quoted.

checks.claim: Context: company's claim that it did not reach the unborn had no support
checks.note: 'claims that the drug did not cross the placental barrier lacked substantiation'.

checks.claim: Context quote: May 1961, 'the burden of proof that the drug is safe' lay with the applicant
checks.note: Letter to Joseph Murray of Merrell, 5 May 1961: 'The burden of proof that the drug is safe ... lies with the applicant.'

checks.claim: Context: Richardson-Merrell withdrew its application in March 1962, after the European birth defects
checks.note: Wikipedia: March 1962; Grokipedia gives 2 or 8 March 1962. 'March 1962' is safe.

checks.claim: The 1938 law asked only that a new drug be shown safe
checks.note: 'The original Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act only required that a new drug be safe.'

checks.claim: Kefauver-Harris Amendments passed by Congress in October 1962
checks.note: Passed by Congress in early October 1962 (voice vote, unanimous); signed by Kennedy 10 October 1962 as Public Law 87-781 (Wikipedia: passed unanimously in October 1962).

checks.claim: Key: evidence from careful studies that it works
checks.note: 21 U.S.C. 355(d): 'substantial evidence' = 'adequate and well-controlled investigations' showing the drug 'will have the effect it purports or is represented to have'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: better than older drugs; approved abroad; costs no more
checks.note: The law requires effect for labelled uses, not superiority (Grokipedia); foreign approval and price are not grounds in 355(d).

checks.claim: Context: informed consent in trials; makers report side effects
checks.note: FDA: patients in trials 'must give their informed consent'; Grokipedia: required 'manufacturers to report adverse reactions'.

checks.claim: Context: Sam Peltzman argued in 1973 that the rules sharply cut new drugs reaching patients
checks.note: Peltzman, 'An Evaluation of Consumer Protection Legislation: The 1962 Drug Amendments', Journal of Political Economy 81(5), September 1973; found new chemical entities fell by more than half (Grokipedia: 43 a year to 16). Attributed, as the stance rule asks.

checks.claim: USPHS began the study in Macon County, Alabama, in 1932 with about 600 Black men, about 400 with syphilis and about 200 without
checks.note: CDC: 600 Black men, 399 with syphilis and 201 without, from 1932, with the Tuskegee Institute.

checks.claim: Told they were treated for 'bad blood', a local term for many ills; free exams and hot meals
checks.note: CDC: 'bad blood', a local term covering several ailments; free medical exams, meals, burial insurance. Wikipedia: hot meals on examination days.

checks.claim: Key: to learn what syphilis does if never treated
checks.note: CDC: to 'observe the natural history of untreated syphilis'; Wikipedia: 'to observe the effects of the disease when untreated, to the point of death and autopsy'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: new drug cure; men given syphilis recovering; vaccine
checks.note: No drug or vaccine was tested; the 399 'were recruited because they already had late-latent syphilis'.

checks.claim: Context: the PHS 'meant to record the natural course ... following the men for the rest of their lives'
checks.note: ASU Embryo Project: researchers 'initially designed the project to last only six to eight months' (followed by treatment, per Grokipedia's 'brief 6-to-8-month observation phase followed by standard treatment'); it was extended indefinitely in late 1932 to 1933 and became a follow-up to death. Read as the 1932 plan, the line is wrong. Fix: 'Planned at first for six to eight months, the study was soon extended to follow the men for the rest of their lives.'

checks.claim: Context: treatments of the day, arsenic and mercury compounds, toxic and only mildly effective; doctors argued the knowledge would help
checks.note: Salvarsan (arsenic), mercurial ointments and bismuth, 'mildly effective and highly toxic'; researchers reasoned 'the knowledge gained would benefit humankind'.

checks.claim: Context: never told they had syphilis; no informed consent; the 399 already had it
checks.note: 'There is no evidence that researchers obtained informed consent from participants'; 399 recruited because they already had late-latent syphilis.

checks.claim: Penicillin the standard cure for syphilis by the late 1940s
checks.note: CDC: treatment of choice by 1943; Wikipedia and Grokipedia: standard by 1947. 'By the late 1940s' is true on either date.

checks.claim: Key: the study doctors did not offer it to the men
checks.note: CDC: 'the participants in the study were not offered treatment'; Wikipedia: 'None of the infected men were treated with penicillin' by the study.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: gave it to every man; to half to compare; offered but refused
checks.note: All contradicted: treatment was withheld from both groups, not offered.

checks.claim: Context: lists of the men given to local doctors in 1934; kept from treatment when drafted in the Second World War
checks.note: Grokipedia: in 1934 the study 'distributed participant lists to local Black physicians'; Wikipedia: of 256 infected men diagnosed at draft induction, 'PHS researchers prevented these men from getting treatment'.

checks.claim: Context: not secret; reports in medical journals for decades
checks.note: 'The study was not secret, since reports and data sets were published to the medical community throughout its duration' (first major report 1936).

checks.claim: Context: 'Dozens of the men died of syphilis or its effects'
checks.note: By 1972, '28 patients had died directly from syphilis' and '100 died from complications related to syphilis' (Wikipedia; Grokipedia the same), about 128 in all. 'Dozens' is true of the 28 but understates 'syphilis or its effects'. Fix: 'By 1972, 28 of the men had died of syphilis and about 100 more of its complications', or 'more than a hundred of the men died of syphilis or its effects'.

checks.claim: Context: some wives and children caught it
checks.note: At least 40 wives infected; 19 children born with congenital syphilis.

checks.claim: Peter Buxtun interviewed patients with venereal diseases for the USPHS in San Francisco
checks.note: Hired December 1965 'to interview patients with sexually transmitted diseases' in San Francisco.

checks.claim: He protested to his superiors in 1966 and again in 1968
checks.note: Protests to the Division of Venereal Diseases in November 1966 and November 1968, both rejected.

checks.claim: 'A committee at the federal Center for Disease Control reviewed the study in 1969 and let it go on'
checks.note: The review and its outcome are right (Grokipedia: the CDC convened a panel in February 1969 that recommended continuing). The name is anachronistic: the agency was the National Communicable Disease Center from 1 July 1967 and became the Center for Disease Control only on 24 June 1970 (CDC timeline; Wikipedia, CDC timeline). Minor. Fix: 'A committee at the federal agency now called the Centers for Disease Control (CDC) reviewed the study in 1969' or 'at the National Communicable Disease Center'.

checks.claim: Key: a news story that made it public ended the study in 1972
checks.note: CDC: the study ended on the recommendation of an Ad Hoc Advisory Panel 'convened after news articles about the study were published'.

checks.claim: Wrong choices: court order; new law by Congress; death of the last man
checks.note: Class action filed 1973 (after the end), National Research Act 1974, last participant died 2004 (Wikipedia).

checks.claim: Context: the 1969 committee saw a unique chance to study late syphilis
checks.note: Grokipedia: the panel saw 'the unique opportunity to study untreated late-stage syphilis'.

checks.claim: Context: 'Buxtun then passed the story to Jean Heller of the Associated Press'
checks.note: Wikipedia (Peter Buxtun) says he leaked to Heller; the AP's own 50-year account says Buxtun gave the papers to AP reporter Edith Lederer in San Francisco, who handed them to Heller at the 1972 Democratic convention. Facts.md itself says the bank would avoid this. Fix: 'Buxtun then passed his papers to the Associated Press, and Jean Heller's report ran on 25 July 1972'.

checks.claim: Context: Heller's report ran on 25 July 1972
checks.note: Washington Star, 25 July 1972; New York Times front page the next day.

checks.claim: Context quote: an advisory panel judged the study 'ethically unjustified'; ended 16 November 1972; 74 men alive
checks.note: CDC: the Ad Hoc Advisory Panel found the study 'ethically unjustified' and advised stopping it in October 1972; Wikipedia and Grokipedia: ended 16 November 1972; 'only 74 of the test subjects were still alive'.

checks.claim: Context: the lawsuit and the new law came afterwards
checks.note: Class action 1973, settled for $10 million in 1974; National Research Act 12 July 1974.

checks.claim: Congress passed the National Research Act in 1974, after Tuskegee came to light
checks.note: Signed by Nixon on 12 July 1974; it 'gained traction as a response to the infamous Tuskegee syphilis study'.

checks.claim: Under the rules that grew from it, nearly all federally funded research on people needs approval before it begins
checks.note: 45 CFR 46 requires IRB review of federally funded human-subjects research, but 46.104 exempts eight bounded categories (some surveys, interviews, educational tests, public observation, certain secondary research...). 'Nearly all' is a fair child-level simplification of non-exempt research; 'most' would be safer.

checks.claim: Key: a review board that weighs its ethics (IRB)
checks.note: Federal regulations 'mandate Institutional Review Boards (IRBs) for oversight of human subjects research funded by federal agencies'; the act 'formalized a regulated IRB process' (Wikipedia, National Research Act).

checks.claim: Wrong choices: Surgeon General; a federal judge; the scientists' own professional society
checks.note: None approves research under 45 CFR 46; approval is by an IRB.

checks.claim: Context: IRBs include members from outside science; weigh risks; check informed consent (told the truth, understanding, free to say no)
checks.note: 46.107: 'at least one member whose primary concerns are in nonscientific areas' and one not affiliated with the institution. Belmont: consent = information, comprehension, voluntariness (Grokipedia). 'Each institution keeps an IRB' is a simplification (an institution may rely on another's IRB) but fine for the grade.

checks.claim: Context: the commission the act set up 'wrote the Belmont Report in 1979'
checks.note: The National Commission completed the report and sent it to the HEW Secretary on 30 September 1978; it was published in the Federal Register on 18 April 1979 (HHS OHRP; Grokipedia). It was written by 1978 and published in 1979. Minor. Fix: 'The commission the act set up issued the Belmont Report, published in 1979, ...'.

checks.claim: Context: Belmont principles are respect for persons, beneficence and justice
checks.note: 'respect for persons, beneficence, and justice'.

unit_notes: Two substantive errors: 7dcdd22bd0 (Evans did not chair the committee that set the 1941 radium tolerance level; L. F. Curtiss of the National Bureau of Standards chaired it, per NBS Handbook 27 and Coursey, J. Res. NIST 2021; only the DOE ACHRE report names Evans chairman) and ac5ccbf81a's card (the 1938 law let the FDA refuse a drug not shown safe; the problem was the automatic 60-day approval, per Weinberger v. Hynson and UChicago Medicine; the card also contradicts the next card's 'burden of proof' quote). Two minor errors (wording fixes): 033edf1190 names the 1969 agency 'Center for Disease Control' a year before it took that name; 25515aa098 says the Belmont Report was written in 1979 (completed September 1978, published April 1979). Three uncertain: 026cc989e2 (the study was planned for 6 to 8 months at first, so 'for the rest of their lives' should not read as the 1932 plan), 7d2b959afb ('dozens' died understates the usual 28 plus 100 from complications), 033edf1190 (Buxtun reached Heller through AP's Edith Lederer, per the AP). Everything the brief asked to check hard (radium as calcium in bone; the Drinker report altered to 'every girl is in perfect condition'; the Fryer settlement, 4 June 1928; Donohue, 5 April 1938; 0.1 microgram in the body; the rodent tests and the 'non-toxic' claim; Kelsey's grounds and the Florence letter of 31 December 1960; the 1962 proof of efficacy; 600/399/201; penicillin by 1943 to 1947; Heller's 25 July 1972 story; the National Research Act, IRBs, the Belmont principles) checks out apart from the points above.
